claim: Telomerase extends telomere sequences at chromosomal ends to protect genomic DNA.
source: Telomerase extends telomere sequences at chromosomal ends to protect genomic DNA.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract describing the function of telomerase, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Structures of Tribolium castaneum telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) throughout its catalytic cycle were determined.
source: Here, we determined structures of Tribolium castaneum telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) throughout its catalytic cycle and mapped the active site residues responsible for nucleoside selection, metal coordination, triphosphate binding, and RNA template stabilization.
evidence: The manuscript describes structural determination work performed by the authors, as evidenced by crystallographic data and figures.

claim: TERT inserts a mismatch approximately 1 in 10,000 insertion events.
source: We found that TERT inserts a mismatch or ribonucleotide ~1 in 10,000 and ~1 in 14,000 insertion events, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by pre-steady-state kinetic measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: TERT inserts a ribonucleotide approximately 1 in 14,000 insertion events.
source: We found that TERT inserts a mismatch or ribonucleotide ~1 in 10,000 and ~1 in 14,000 insertion events, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by pre-steady-state kinetic measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: At biological ribonucleotide concentrations, telomerase inserts approximately 40 ribonucleotides per 10 kilobases.
source: At biological ribonucleotide concentrations, these rates translate to ~40 ribonucleotides inserted per 10 kilobases.
evidence: This is calculated from kinetic data combined with known cellular nucleotide concentrations.

claim: A conserved tyrosine steric gate regulates ribonucleotide insertion into telomeres.
source: Human telomerase assays determined a conserved tyrosine steric gate regulates ribonucleotide insertion into telomeres.
evidence: This is supported by both tcTERT kinetic data and human telomerase activity assays showing Y256/Y717 function.

claim: During every round of eukaryotic cell division, a small amount of DNA is lost from the ends of each chromosome.
source: During every round of eukaryotic cell division, a small amount of DNA is lost from the ends of each chromosome (Olovnikov, 1973; Watson, 1972).
evidence: This is a well-established phenomenon in cell biology, supported by citations to foundational work.

claim: Repetitive noncoding DNA sequences known as telomeres are found at chromosomal ends.
source: First, repetitive noncoding DNA sequences, known as telomeres, are found at chromosomal ends, preventing the loss of vital genetic information during each cell division (Blackburn and Gall, 1978; Moyzis et al., 1988).
evidence: This is established knowledge about telomere structure and function, supported by citations.

claim: Telomerase elongates shortened telomeres at chromosomal ends using a reverse transcriptase activity.
source: Second, the ribonucleoprotein telomerase elongates shortened telomeres at chromosomal ends using a reverse transcriptase activity (Greider and Blackburn, 1987).
evidence: This is a fundamental property of telomerase, supported by citation to the original discovery.

claim: Without telomere elongation, telomeres will eventually reach a critically short length, causing cells to undergo apoptosis or become senescent.
source: Without elongation, telomeres will eventually reach a critically short length, causing cells to undergo apoptosis or become senescent (Hayflick and Moorhead, 1961; Meyerson, 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cellular responses to telomere shortening, supported by citations.

claim: Approximately 90% of cancers upregulate telomerase to combat telomere shortening and enable unlimited cell division.
source: In particular,~90% of cancers upregulate telomerase to combat telomere shortening and enable unlimited cell division, as opposed to somatic cells where telomerase is absent (Jafri et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a well-documented phenomenon in cancer biology, supported by citation.

claim: Catalysis in telomerase is localized to the telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) subunit.
source: Although the human telomerase holoenzyme is composed of multiple accessory subunits, catalysis is localized to the telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) subunit (Nguyen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural and functional studies of telomerase.

claim: The highest resolution structural snapshot of human telomerase is a cryo-EM structure at 8 Å resolution.
source: Currently, the highest resolution structural snapshot of human telomerase is a cryo-EM structure at 8 Å resolution (Nguyen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the state of structural biology at the time of writing, supported by citation.

claim: tcTERT readily fits into the cryo-EM density of hTERT.
source: first, tcTERT readily fit into the cryo-EM density of hTERT and aligns well with the recent cryo-EM structure from T. thermophila, highlighting the conserved secondary structure (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The active site pocket of tcTERT exhibits a high degree of sequence identity with hTERT.
source: second, upon alignment with hTERT, the active site pocket of tcTERT exhibits a high degree of sequence identity (Supplementary file 1, Table 1a)
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data presented in Supplementary file 1, Table 1a.

claim: tcTERT lacks the N-terminal (TEN) domain.
source: These include tcTERT lacking the N-terminal (TEN) domain and missing a portion of the insertion in fingers domain (IFD) (Supplementary file 1, Table 1b).
evidence: This is a structural comparison between tcTERT and hTERT, documented in supplementary data.

claim: tcTERT is missing a portion of the insertion in fingers domain (IFD).
source: These include tcTERT lacking the N-terminal (TEN) domain and missing a portion of the insertion in fingers domain (IFD) (Supplementary file 1, Table 1b).
evidence: This is a structural comparison between tcTERT and hTERT, documented in supplementary data.

claim: Telomerase forms a prenucleotide bound binary complex (State A1).
source: First, telomerase anneals its RNA template to the end of telomeric DNA to form a binary complex (TERT:DNA, Figure 1A, state A1).
evidence: This is part of the catalytic cycle description, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The binary complex binds an incoming dNTP to form a ternary complex.
source: Next, the binary complex binds an incoming dNTP and samples for proper Watson-Crick base pairing to the RNA template (Figure 1A, state B1).
evidence: This is part of the catalytic cycle description, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: TERT catalyzes the formation of a phosphodiester bond to extend the telomere by one nucleotide.
source: If the resulting ternary complex (TERT:DNA:dNTP) is in the proper orientation, TERT will catalyze the formation of a phosphodiester bond and extend the telomere by one nucleotide (Figure 1A, state C1).
evidence: This describes the chemistry step of the catalytic cycle, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Telomerase becomes inactive after two repeats but can be reactivated by intracellular telomerase-activating factors (iTAFs).
source: It was recently shown telomerase becomes inactive after two repeats, but can be reactivated by the recently discovered intracellular telomerase-activating factors (iTAFs) (Sayed et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a recent finding about telomerase regulation, supported by citation.

claim: The prenucleotide binary complex structure was determined at 2.5 Å resolution.
source: Crystals of this complex grew in a P3221 space group, diffracting to 2.5 Å resolution (Supplementary file 2, Table 2a).
evidence: This is crystallographic data from the structure determination.

claim: TERT binds as a ring around the end of the RNA:DNA complex.
source: The resulting structure shows TERT bound as a ring around the end of the RNA:DNA complex, with its active site positioned at the terminus of the DNA strand (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure, shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Residues I196, V197, S198, G309, and R194 compose a pocket around the templating RNA base.
source: Residues I196, V197, S198, G309, and R194 compose a pocket around the templating RNA base (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Side chains from T341 and V342 coordinate the deoxyribose sugar moiety of the 3'-dA with nonpolar interactions.
source: On the opposite side, the 3'-OH of the primer terminal 3'-dA points towards the catalytic metal binding site, and side chains from T341 and V342 coordinate the deoxyribose sugar moiety of the 3'-dA with nonpolar interactions (Figure 1E and Supplementary file 1, Table 1a).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure, shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The nucleoside binding group is composed of residues R194, Y256, and Q308.
source: The nucleoside binding group is composed of residues R194, Y256, and Q308 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure, shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The catalytic residues include the catalytic triad: D251, D343, and D344.
source: The catalytic residues include the catalytic triad: D251, D343, and D344.
evidence: This is a structural observation identifying the catalytic residues.

claim: Residues K189, A255, N369, and the backbone of K372 are in position to form interactions with the triphosphate of the incoming nucleotide.
source: Residues K189, A255, N369, and the backbone of K372 are in position to form interactions with the triphosphate of the incoming nucleotide (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure, shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The ternary complex crystals grew in the P3221 space group and diffracted to 2.9 Å resolution.
source: Crystals of this complex grew in the same P3221 space group and diffracted to 2.9 Å resolution (Supplementary file 2, Table 2a).
evidence: This is crystallographic data from the structure determination.

claim: Minimal structural rearrangements are required for TERT to bind dGpCpp, with an RMSD value of 1.52 Å between binary and ternary complexes.
source: Comparing this ternary complex to the binary state (RMSD value of 1.52 Å, Figure 2A) indicates minimal structural rearrangements are required for TERT to bind dGpCpp.
evidence: This is a quantitative structural comparison based on crystallographic data.

claim: Two Mg2+ ions exhibit octahedral coordination to facilitate nucleotide binding.
source: Two Mg+2 ions exhibit octahedral coordination to facilitate nucleotide binding.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the ternary complex crystal structure.

claim: The catalytic metal coordinates residues D251, D343, D344, the 3'-OH of the primer terminus, and the non-bridging oxygen of the dGpCpp α-phosphate.
source: The catalytic metal coordinates residues D251, D343, D344, the 3'-OH of the primer terminus, and the non-bridging oxygen of the dGpCpp α-phosphate (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the ternary complex, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The nucleotide metal coordinates the side chains of D251 and D343, the backbone carbonyl of I252, and a non-bridging oxygen on the α, β, and γ phosphates of the incoming dGpCpp.
source: The nucleotide metal coordinates the side chains of D251 and D343, the backbone carbonyl of I252, and a non-bridging oxygen on the α,β, and γ phosphates of the incoming dGpCpp (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the ternary complex, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Y256 is positioned near the C2 position of the deoxyribose sugar portion of the nucleoside.
source: Y256 is positioned near the C2 position of the deoxyribose sugar portion of the nucleoside, and Q308 coordinates the nucleoside component of the dGpCpp (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the ternary complex, shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Minimal structural changes are observed between the prenucleotide binary complex and the product structure, with an RMSD value of 1.04 Å.
source: Both globally and within the active site, we observed minimal structural changes between the prenucleotide binary complex and the product structure (RMSD value of 1.04 Å, Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a quantitative structural comparison based on crystallographic data.

claim: TERT inserts correctly matched dGTP across from a templating rC with a kpol of 1.05 s−1.
source: TERT inserts the correctly matched dGTP across from a templating rC with a kpol of 1.05 s−1 and a Kd for the incoming dGTP of 18.1 μM (Figure 3A,D).
evidence: This is kinetic data from pre-steady-state experiments, shown in Figure 3A,D.

claim: TERT inserts correctly matched dGTP across from a templating rC with a Kd of 18.1 μM.
source: TERT inserts the correctly matched dGTP across from a templating rC with a kpol of 1.05 s−1 and a Kd for the incoming dGTP of 18.1 μM (Figure 3A,D).
evidence: This is kinetic data from pre-steady-state experiments, shown in Figure 3A,D.

claim: For TERT R194A, the kpol decreased by 28-fold to 0.0369 s−1.
source: For TERT R194A, the kpol decreased by 28-fold to 0.0369 s−1, and the Kd for dGTP increased ~5 fold to 93 μM (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,C).
evidence: This is kinetic data from pre-steady-state experiments with the R194A mutant.

claim: For TERT R194A, the Kd for dGTP increased approximately 5-fold to 93 μM.
source: For TERT R194A, the kpol decreased by 28-fold to 0.0369 s−1, and the Kd for dGTP increased ~5 fold to 93 μM (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,C).
evidence: This is kinetic data from pre-steady-state experiments with the R194A mutant.

claim: With the Q308A variant, the kpol decreased approximately 60-fold to 0.30 s−1.
source: With the Q308A variant, the kpol decreased ~60 fold to 0.30 s−1 and the Kd for dGTP increased ~2 fold to 45 μM (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,D).
evidence: This is kinetic data from pre-steady-state experiments with the Q308A mutant.

claim: With the Q308A variant, the Kd for dGTP increased approximately 2-fold to 45 μM.
source: With the Q308A variant, the kpol decreased ~60 fold to 0.30 s−1 and the Kd for dGTP increased ~2 fold to 45 μM (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,D).
evidence: This is kinetic data from pre-steady-state experiments with the Q308A mutant.

claim: R194 and Q308 primarily play a role in the chemistry step rather than nucleotide binding.
source: Therefore, R194 and Q308 primarily play a role in the chemistry step rather than the nucleotide binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data showing larger effects on kpol than Kd.

claim: The hTERT homolog to R194 (R631) is implicated in IPF.
source: As the hTERT homolog to R194 (R631, Supplementary file 1, Table 1a) is implicated in IPF, we infer that mutations at R631 likely reduce hTERT's kpol, contributing to IPF pathologies (Basel-Vanagaite et al., 2008; Diaz de Leon et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations linking R631 mutations to IPF and inference from the kinetic data.

claim: For mismatched dATP insertion opposite templating rC, the kpol decreased 129-fold to 0.0081 s−1.
source: For the mismatched insertion, the kpol decreased 129-fold to 0.0081 s−1 and the Kd increased 76-fold to 1.3 mM (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is kinetic data from pre-steady-state experiments measuring fidelity.

claim: For mismatched dATP insertion opposite templating rC, the Kd increased 76-fold to 1.3 mM.
source: For the mismatched insertion, the kpol decreased 129-fold to 0.0081 s−1 and the Kd increased 76-fold to 1.3 mM (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is kinetic data from pre-steady-state experiments measuring fidelity.

claim: Telomerase will insert the wrong nucleotide approximately 1 in 10,000 nucleotide insertion events.
source: The resulting catalytic efficiencies (kpol/Kd) for a matched versus mismatched nucleotide insertion indicate telomerase will insert the wrong nucleotide ~1 in 10,000 nucleotide insertion events.
evidence: This is calculated from the catalytic efficiency ratios obtained from kinetic data.

claim: For rGTP insertion, the kpol decreased 281-fold to 0.0037 s−1.
source: For rNTP discrimination, the kpol for inserting a rGTP decreased 281-fold to 0.0037 s−1 and the Kd increased 49-fold to 0.89 mM (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is kinetic data from pre-steady-state experiments measuring sugar discrimination.

claim: For rGTP insertion, the Kd increased 49-fold to 0.89 mM.
source: For rNTP discrimination, the kpol for inserting a rGTP decreased 281-fold to 0.0037 s−1 and the Kd increased 49-fold to 0.89 mM (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is kinetic data from pre-steady-state experiments measuring sugar discrimination.

claim: There is a nearly 14,000-fold decrease in the catalytic efficiency for the insertion of a rNTP compared to a dNTP.
source: This results in a nearly 14,000-fold decrease in the catalytic efficiency for the insertion of a rNTP compared to a dNTP (i.e. sugar discrimination, Figure 3H).
evidence: This is calculated from the catalytic efficiency ratios obtained from kinetic data.

claim: Telomerase will insert a rNTP approximately 1 in 280 insertion events in a cellular context.
source: Because the cellular concentrations of rNTPs are around 50-fold higher on average than dNTPs, this sugar discrimination indicates telomerase will insert a rNTP ~1 in 280 insertion events in a cellular context (see discussion) (Traut, 1994).
evidence: This is calculated from kinetic data adjusted for known cellular nucleotide concentrations.

claim: Y256 rests in the minor groove of the DNA and is in position to clash with the 2'-OH of an incoming rNTP.
source: Throughout the TERT catalytic cycle, we observed that Y256 rests in the minor groove of the DNA and is in position to clash with the 2'-OH of an incoming rNTP (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structures.

claim: For TERT Y256A inserting rGTP, the kpol increased 1,490-fold to 5.5 s−1 compared to WT TERT.
source: Compared to WT TERT, the insertion of a matched rGTP by Y256A showed a 1,490-fold increase in kpol to 5.5 s−1 and a 12-fold decrease in Kd to 73 μM (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is kinetic data from pre-steady-state experiments with the Y256A mutant.

claim: For TERT Y256A inserting rGTP, the Kd decreased 12-fold to 73 μM compared to WT TERT.
source: Compared to WT TERT, the insertion of a matched rGTP by Y256A showed a 1,490-fold increase in kpol to 5.5 s−1 and a 12-fold decrease in Kd to 73 μM (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is kinetic data from pre-steady-state experiments with the Y256A mutant.

claim: For TERT Y256A inserting dGTP, the kpol is 6.6 s−1 and the Kd is 74 μM.
source: The results for TERT Y256A inserting a matched dGTP were similar to that of the rGTP, with a kpol and Kd of 6.6 s−1 and 74 μM, respectively (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is kinetic data from pre-steady-state experiments with the Y256A mutant.

claim: The sugar selectivity of TERT dropped from 14,000-fold for WT TERT to less than 2-fold for the Y256A TERT variant.
source: Thus, the sugar selectivity of TERT dropped from 14,000-fold between rGTP and dGTP for WT TERT to less than 2-fold for the Y256A TERT variant (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is calculated from the catalytic efficiency ratios for WT and Y256A mutant.

claim: A single Y256A substitution increased rGTP insertion efficiency by 18,000-fold.
source: In other words, a single Y256A substitution increased rGTP insertion efficiency by 18,000-fold, abolishing almost all sugar discrimination.
evidence: This is calculated from the change in catalytic efficiency between WT and Y256A.

claim: Under cellular conditions, WT TERT would insert rGTP over 100-fold times less efficiently than dGTP.
source: In a cellular environment, where rNTPs are at much higher concentrations than dNTPs, WT TERT would insert rGTP over 100-fold times less efficiently than dGTP.
evidence: This is calculated from kinetic data adjusted for cellular nucleotide concentrations.

claim: Under cellular conditions, TERT Y256A would insert rGTP 77-fold times more efficiently than dGTP.
source: In contrast, TERT Y256A under cellular conditions would insert rGTP 77-fold times more efficiently than dGTP (Figure 4F; Traut, 1994).
evidence: This is calculated from kinetic data adjusted for cellular nucleotide concentrations.

claim: The distance from the C2 carbon of the dGpCpp to residue 256 shifted from 3.3 Å in WT TERT to 5.7 Å in TERT Y256A.
source: The distance from the C2 carbon of the dGpCpp to residue 256 shifted from 3.3 Å in WT TERT to 5.7 Å in TERT Y256A, showing that the TERT Y256A has much more room to accommodate the 2'-OH (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is a structural measurement from the Y256A crystal structure compared to WT.

claim: Y256 clashes with the 2'-OH of rNTPs to provide sugar discrimination and is the steric gate in telomerase.
source: Taken as a whole, these results indicate Y256 clashes with the 2'-OH of rNTPs to provide sugar discrimination and is the steric gate in telomerase.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined structural and kinetic data on Y256A.

claim: WT telomerase showed approximately 10% primer extension in the presence of dNTPs over 30 minutes.
source: WT telomerase showed robust primer extension in the presence of dNTPs, with ~10% of the primer extended into product over the course of 30 min (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is data from human telomerase activity assays shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: With all four dNTPs, the Y717A variant reached approximately 7% primer extension in 30 minutes.
source: Similarly, with all four dNTPs, the Y717A variant reached ~7% primer extension in the same amount of time (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is data from human telomerase activity assays shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: When WT telomerase was incubated with all four rNTPs, very low (<1%) primer extension was observed after 30 minutes.
source: In contrast, when we incubated WT telomerase with all four rNTPs rather than dNTPs, we observed very low (<1%) primer extension after 30 min, suggesting that human telomerase discriminates against rNTPs, similar to tcTERT (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is data from human telomerase activity assays shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The Y717A variant showed 3-fold increased primer extension compared to WT hTERT in the presence of rNTPs.
source: When we performed the same telomeric extension assay with the steric gate variant (Y717A), we observed that the primer extension was increased 3-fold compared to WT hTERT in the presence of rNTPs (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is data from human telomerase activity assays shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Y717 in hTERT is the steric gate in human telomerase.
source: These results indicate the conserved residue Y717 in hTERT (Supplementary file 1, Table 1a) is the steric gate in human telomerase.
evidence: This is concluded from the human telomerase activity assays with Y717A mutant.

claim: The presence of rNTPs in telomere strands may inhibit the telomerase translocation step.
source: Interestingly, in both WT and Y717A telomerase, minimal insertion past the first telomeric repeat was observed, which suggests the presence of rNTPs in telomere strands may inhibit the telomerase translocation step (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of extension products in the activity assays.

claim: Telomerase processivity was reduced when one rNTP was substituted into the nucleotide mix at a time.
source: By substituting one rNTP into the nucleotide mix at a time, we could determine the effects of inserting one, two, or three rNTPs inserted per repeat (with rATP, rUTP, and rGTP, respectively). In each case, telomerase processivity was reduced, with no bands evident past the second telomeric repeat (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is data from human telomerase activity assays shown in Figure 5E.

claim: For the Y717A mutant telomerase, the effects of rNTPs on telomerase's processivity were much less pronounced.
source: For the steric gate Y717A mutant telomerase, the effect of rNTPs on telomerase's processivity were much less pronounced.
evidence: This is observed from the activity assay data comparing WT and Y717A with rNTPs.

claim: rNTPs inhibited translocation in both Y717A and WT telomerase.
source: Interestingly, rNTPs inhibited translocation in both Y717A and WT telomerase, implying that telomerase possesses rNTP discrimination mechanisms beyond the level of single nucleotide incorporations (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of extension products in the activity assays.

claim: Minimal global rearrangement is required for TERT to proceed through the catalytic cycle.
source: In this study, we characterized each step of the TERT catalytic cycle for single nucleotide insertion. We found that, in terms of global protein structure, minimal rearrangement is required to proceed through the catalytic cycle.
evidence: This is concluded from the structural comparisons showing low RMSD values between states.

claim: TERT does not undergo global shifts from an 'open' to a 'closed' state upon nucleotide binding, unlike many other DNA polymerases.
source: This lack of rearrangement contrasts many other DNA polymerases and even HIV RT, which have been shown to undergo global shifts from an 'open' to a 'closed' state upon nucleotide binding (Doublié et al., 1999; Sawaya et al., 1994; Schmidt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison to other polymerases based on structural observations and citations.

claim: Telomerase exhibits moderate base selection fidelity, similar to X-family polymerases involved in DNA repair.
source: While telomerase has been shown to exhibit moderate base and position-specific effects, our results indicate that the telomerase catalytic core generally exhibits moderate base selection fidelity, similar to that of X-family polymerases involved in DNA repair (Chen et al., 2018; McCulloch and Kunkel, 2008).
evidence: This is concluded from the fidelity measurements and comparison to other polymerases.

claim: Telomerase inserts approximately 1 mismatch per 10 kb of telomere extension.
source: Based on our kinetic values, we predict that telomerase inserts ~ 1 mismatch per each 10 kb of telomere extension.
evidence: This is calculated from the fidelity measurements.

claim: Telomerase does not have a proofreading domain.
source: Because telomerase does not have a proofreading domain, misinsertions created by telomerase will remain as ssDNA during telomere elongation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about telomerase structure and function.

claim: The predicted error rate agrees with telomeric error rates observed using telomere sequencing.
source: Accordingly, our predicted error rate agrees with telomeric error rates observed using telomere sequencing (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison of the calculated error rate to published sequencing data.

claim: Telomeric mismatches likely would disrupt G-quadruplex stability and inhibit shelterin protein binding.
source: While the downstream consequences of telomeric mismatches have not been studied in a biological context to our knowledge, they likely would disrupt G-quadruplex stability and inhibit shelterin protein binding, as both of these phenomena are dependent on DNA sequence (Figure 6B; Burge et al., 2006; de Lange, 2005).
evidence: This is inferred from known sequence-dependence of G-quadruplexes and shelterin binding, supported by citations.

claim: For every 10 kb of telomere extension, telomerase inserts approximately 40 rNTPs.
source: Instead, we predict that for every 10 kb of telomere extension, telomerase inserts ~ 40 rNTPs, which represents selectivity comparable to DNA polymerase β and DNA polymerase δ (Brown and Suo, 2011; Cavanaugh et al., 2010; Nick McElhinny et al., 2010).
evidence: This is calculated from the sugar discrimination measurements adjusted for cellular conditions.

claim: Telomere elongation was reduced via an inhibition of the translocation step even with increased rates of ribonucleotide insertion at the single nucleotide insertion level.
source: In our experiments with human telomerase, we found that even with increased rates of ribonucleotide insertion at the single nucleotide insertion level, telomere elongation was reduced via an inhibition of the translocation step (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is observed from the human telomerase activity assays.

claim: Telomeric substrates containing ribonucleotides can prevent or reduce extension of the first repeat depending on the number and position of ribonucleotides present in the DNA template.
source: Furthermore, previous studies have found telomeric substrates containing ribonucleotides can prevent or reduce extension of the first repeat depending on the number and position of ribonucleotides present in the DNA template (Collins and Greider, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Telomerase may pause after inserting ribonucleotides to provide an opportunity for an extrinsic proofreader or RER to remove the ribonucleotide before continuing telomeric elongation.
source: It is possible that telomerase pauses after inserting ribonucleotides to provide an opportunity for an extrinsic proofreader or RER to remove the ribonucleotide before continuing telomeric elongation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed pausing behavior.

claim: Telomerase has previously been observed to halt telomeric extension after the insertion of 8-oxodeoxyguanine triphosphate (8-oxodGTP).
source: Telomerase has previously been observed to halt telomeric extension after the insertion of other noncanonical nucleotides, particularly in the case of 8-oxodeoxyguanine triphosphate (8-oxodGTP) insertion (Fouquerel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: RNA is more vulnerable to hydrolysis than DNA.
source: Because RNA is more vulnerable to hydrolysis than DNA, inserted ribonucleotides are more likely to hydrolyze, which would cause a telomeric single strand break (Baumann and Cech, 2001; de Lange, 2005; Li and Breaker, 1999).
evidence: This is established chemical knowledge about RNA stability, supported by citations.

claim: Inserted ribonucleotides in telomeres are more likely to hydrolyze, which would cause a telomeric single strand break.
source: Because RNA is more vulnerable to hydrolysis than DNA, inserted ribonucleotides are more likely to hydrolyze, which would cause a telomeric single strand break (Baumann and Cech, 2001; de Lange, 2005; Li and Breaker, 1999).
evidence: This is inferred from the chemical properties of RNA and potential consequences in telomeres.

claim: The continued presence of ribonucleotides in telomeres may alter G-quadruplex stability and disrupt shelterin protein binding.
source: The continued presence of ribonucleotides in telomeres may cause several structural aberrations, including altering G-quadruplex stability and disrupting shelterin protein binding (Fay et al., 2017; Nowotny et al., 2005).
evidence: This is inferred from structural studies of ribonucleotides in DNA, supported by citations.

claim: Subtle alterations to the telomeric nucleotides have previously been shown to cause telomeric disruption in a cellular context.
source: Subtle alterations to the telomeric nucleotides have previously been shown to cause telomeric disruption in a cellular context (Fouquerel et al., 2016; Mender et al., 2015; Stefl et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous cellular studies.

claim: The telomerase active site appears to have evolved a high degree of stringency towards noncanonical nucleotides, including both rNTPs and mismatched dNTPs.
source: Therefore, in order to prevent this telomeric disruption, the telomerase active site appears to have evolved a high degree of stringency towards noncanonical nucleotides, including both rNTPs and mismatched dNTPs.
evidence: This is inferred from the fidelity and sugar discrimination measurements.

claim: The active site residues that compose the nucleotide binding pocket are 100% conserved between hTERT and tcTERT.
source: Notably, the residues that compose these three groups are 100% conserved between hTERT and tcTERT (Supplementary file 1, Table 1a).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment data presented in the supplementary materials.

claim: Telomerase will shift registry to align the active site with the next templating base after nucleotide insertion.
source: Following insertion of the incoming nucleotide, telomerase will shift registry to align the active site with the next templating base (forming state A2).
evidence: This is part of the catalytic cycle description based on established knowledge of telomerase function.

claim: The core catalytic cycle repeats six times until a new telomeric repeat is added.
source: This core catalytic cycle repeats six times, until a new telomeric repeat is added (Figure 1A, state C6).
evidence: This is based on the known structure of telomeric repeats and the catalytic cycle.

claim: As telomerase approaches the end of its template, the DNA:RNA duplex at the 5' end begins to melt.
